deep.reconstruction:
PART A (top three lines, end of the uniformization note begun on p.33). The sentence completes: '...the boundary [of the space of Riemann surfaces of genus p, described by the Noether-Weber-Klein canonical normal curve in P^{p-1} and Noether's quadratic relations] must correspond to the boundary which one finds when one writes down the conditions that 2 opposite circular arcs of the Poincaré polygon go over into each other (in sich übergehen).' In modern terms: to prove existence of Fuchsian (Poincaré) uniformization, compare two spaces of real dimension 6p-6. One is the moduli of algebraic curves of genus p, via canonical curves. The other is the space of Fuchsian circular-arc polygons, cut out by the side-pairing conditions: opposite sides must be identified by Möbius transformations. One then shows the map between them is a bijection by matching their boundaries. This is the Klein-Poincaré 'continuity method' (Kontinuitätsmethode). It is only sketched, with no computation.

PART B (pasted slip; a new topic, local/p-adic algebra in Kronecker's 'modular system' language). Read with the corrected transcription: i is an adjoined element with i^p = p, i.e. a root of the Eisenstein polynomial t^p - p.

(1) Question: is x^p - p x - p irreducible with respect to the modulus (i^p - p, p) (and presumably its powers (i^p - p, p^r))? In modern terms: does the Eisenstein polynomial x^p - p x - p remain irreducible over K = Q_p(p^{1/p}), or at least have no root there?

(2) Method proposed: 'to this end one first establishes that x^p [i.e. the reduction of the polynomial] splits modulo (i^p, p) into pure linear factors'. Indeed, modulo p we have x^p - px - p ≡ x^p = x·x·...·x. So the question is whether this trivial factorization lifts to higher powers of p (a Hensel-type lifting question), which it cannot do naively, because the root is repeated.

(3) Generalization: which degree-p polynomials of the form x^p + p·φ(x) (Eisenstein-type) can be split into linear factors with the help of i^p - p and p^r? That is: which ones split over Q_p(p^{1/p}) modulo every p^r? Which ones split with the help of i^p - p i - p, i.e. over Q_p(β) with β^p - pβ - p = 0?

(4) Final question: how many such auxiliary polynomials (adjoined to the modulus) are needed so that every polynomial of degree p splits into linear factors modulo every p^r? In modern terms: what is the compositum of all degree-p extensions of Q_p, and how many generators does it need? Implicitly this asserts that finitely many suffice, i.e. that Q_p has only finitely many extensions of degree p.

My own completion of question (1). Let α be a root of f = x^p - px - p and π = p^{1/p}. Both are Eisenstein, so totally ramified of degree p over Q_p.
- For f: f'(α) = p(α^{p-1} - 1). Since α^{p-1} - 1 is a unit, v_p(f'(α)) = 1 and v_p(disc f) = p.
- For x^p - p: v_p(disc) = v_p(p^p · p^{p-1}) = 2p - 1.
- For Eisenstein polynomials, these are the field discriminant exponents. Since p ≠ 2p - 1, Q_p(α) ≠ Q_p(π).
- Hence f has no root in Q_p(π): it does not split into linear factors modulo all powers of p after adjoining i.
- For p = 2 and p = 3 this already gives irreducibility over Q_p(π), since a reducible polynomial of degree ≤ 3 has a linear factor. For general p, 'no root' does not by itself give irreducibility.
- Example, p = 2: f = x^2 - 2x - 2 has roots 1 ± √3. √3 is not in Q_2(√2), because 3 and 3/2 are not squares in Q_2.
errors: No mathematical errors on the page; it consists of questions, not derivations. The sentence '...dass x^p nach dem Modul (i^p, p) in lauter Linearfactoren' lacks its verb ('zerfällt').

Implicit caution: the factorization mod p (x^p ≡ x^p) is trivial and cannot be lifted by Hensel/Newton because the root is repeated. Settling the question needs a discriminant/ramification argument, which the page does not supply.

Part A is only a programme. The 'continuity method' needs nontrivial topology (invariance of domain, properness), which Hilbert does not address here and which was historically the weak point (Brouwer, Koebe 1912).

results.what: Existence of Fuchsian uniformization by comparing the moduli space of genus-p curves (canonical curves plus Noether's quadratic relations) with the space of Poincaré polygons cut out by side-pairing conditions, matching their boundaries
results.usually_credited_to: Klein and Poincaré (1882-84); rigorous completion by Brouwer and Koebe (1912)

results.what: Question whether the Eisenstein polynomial x^p - px - p is irreducible over the ring obtained by adjoining a root of i^p - p, modulo powers of p
results.modern_name: Irreducibility over / distinctness of totally ramified degree-p extensions of Q_p (Q_p(p^{1/p}) vs Q_p(root of x^p-px-p))
results.usually_credited_to: Hensel (p-adic numbers, 1897-1908); Ore (1920s) on Newton polygons and ramification

results.what: How many auxiliary polynomials must be adjoined so that every polynomial of degree p splits into linear factors modulo every p^r (implicitly: the finiteness of degree-p extensions of Q_p and their compositum)
results.modern_name: Finiteness of extensions of Q_p of given degree; compositum of all degree-p extensions (Krasner's lemma / Krasner's mass formula)

deep.surprise_reason: Dating from the facing page (Hurwitz's 1894/95 proof of prime-ideal decomposition) puts this around 1894-95, before Hensel's p-adic numbers. Hilbert is here formulating local-field questions (splitting of Eisenstein polynomials of degree p modulo p^r, and how many extensions are needed to split all of them) in Kronecker's modular-system language. That is a mildly notable glimpse of proto-local-field thinking, and it fits his work on ramification in Galois number fields (1894). But these are only questions, with no results, so the surprise is modest. The uniformization remark is a known Klein-Poincaré programme.

checkable.sympy: discriminant(x**p - p*x - p, x) for p in [2,3,5] -> [12, -135, -1953125 + ...]; factorint(discriminant(x**3-3*x-3,x)) == {-1:1, 3:3, 5:1}
checkable.asserts: The 3-adic valuation of disc(x^3-3x-3) is 3 (= p).
disc(x^3-3) = -243 = -3^5, so the valuation is 2p-1 = 5. This differs from that of x^3-3x-3, so the cubic fields Q_3(3^{1/3}) and Q_3(root of x^3-3x-3) are distinct.
Modulo p the polynomial reduces to x^p (here x^5), i.e. it splits into p equal linear factors mod p.
The roots are 1 ± sqrt(3), so the case p=2 compares Q_2(sqrt(3)) with Q_2(sqrt(2)).
6 is not a square mod 8 (it is not a 2-adic square), consistent with 3/2 not being a square in Q_2, hence sqrt(3) not in Q_2(sqrt(2)).
x^2-2x-2 stays irreducible over Q(sqrt(2)); a global sanity check consistent with the local claim.

Line 3: 'Modul p(p^2, p)' should probably read 'Modul (i^p, p)'. The leading mark is a stray stroke or cancelled letter.
'mit Hülfe von p^2-p und p^r' should read 'mit Hülfe von i^p - p und p^r'.
'mit Hülfe von p^2-p p-p' should read 'mit Hülfe von i^p - p i - p'.
